newsitem.title: USA: Democrats press Republicans to clear disaster aid.
newsitem.headline: Democrats press Republicans to clear disaster aid.

text.p: Democrats threatened Friday to block all action in the Senate until disaster relief for flood-stricken states is assured and President Clinton again vowed to veto a Republican-backed version.
In reply, House Majority Leader Dick Armey said the president should not object to a key provision backed by Republicans that aims to avert another government shutdown.
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle called callous the Republican decision to delay sending the disaster relief bill to the White House until next week.

Armey said it was being held back to give Clinton time to reconsider. It passed Thursday with two provisions Clinton said are politically unacceptable. Congress would not be in session to vote on a new version until Tuesday.
In a written statement, Clinton urged Congress to send him a straightforward disaster relief bill. "I have no choice but to veto that measure," he said.
"Unfortunately, the Republican leaders of Congress have chosen the path of partisanship and confrontation in their actions on the disaster relief bill," Clinton added.
Republican leaders of both the House and Senate refused to remove two provisions that have drawn a veto threat to the entire $8.6 billion emergency money bill.

The first would guarantee federal agencies funding at the 1997 level if Congress and the White House fail to agree on funding by the Oct. 1 start of the fiscal year. The second would block the use of sampling to include uncounted minorities in the 2000 census.

Daschle, a South Dakota Democrat, told reporters: "We will not allow legislation to move in Congress until this issue is resolved." He said they were undecided whether to block committees from meeting.
His state was one of 35 in need of federal assistance for recovery from weather damage. South Dakota and much of the upper plains were still reeling from floods.
Armey later told a news conference the disaster bill would go to Clinton Monday.

While he argued the anti-shutdown provision would assure neither side held the advantage in coming money battles, Democrats and the White House said it would give Republicans little reason to provide Clinton with the additional funds for education, the environment and other programs that were contained in the budget deal just passed by Congress.

"I don't know why he wants to preserve the right to have a shutdown," Armey, a Texas Republican, said. Republicans are still stinging from the 1995 government shutdowns that polls showed was a political fiasco for them.

The bill provides $5.4 billion for disaster assistance, including $89 million for House Speaker Newt Gingrich's home state of Georgia and $24 million for Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott's state of Mississippi.

Rebutting Republican claims that there was money in the federal pipeline to provide emergency relief, Daschle insisted there were no funds available to begin permanent recovery. Money is needed by farmers to start rebuilding herds, by homeowners who await buyouts of homes in flood plains and by businesses to rebuild their inventories, he said.

The bill also contained $1.9 billion to pay for military operations in Bosnia and the Gulf and $262 million for feeding poor women and their children, for education and for a new transportation system at Yosemite National Park.
